description: Hola, Soy Josue Morales, ingeniero de software cambiando su enfoque a tecnología para la salud con ayuda de la Inteligencia Artificial, actualmente trabajo en backend y arquitectura de software, pero como hobby estoy construyendo PeWoNu, una plataforma de bienestar basada en tres pilares: Peace (salud mental), Wod (entrenamiento físico) y Nutrition (nutrición), la idea es aplicar ese enfoque a este reto.
summary: PeWoNu (Peace, WOD, Nutrition) is a wellbeing prototype for astronauts on long missions, built with simulated, analog data. Instead of comparing an astronaut with an average person, it compares them with their own baseline, kept separately for Earth, the spacecraft and a planet's surface, and it shows gray when it does not have enough data instead of guessing. It has three pillars. Peace: a five-face mood check, a guided manual-pulse mission that teaches the wrist technique, and an optional voice log that discards the audio and keeps only numbers. WOD: a workout of the day on the three ISS machines (T2, CEVIS and ARED) from age, weight and bone density. Nutrition: a daily energy estimate next to the 1,900 to 3,200 kcal range used by station dietitians, and a meal log by ISS food type. Each body system is colored against the baseline, with a card that explains why. The rules are deterministic: no AI model is in the alert path and nothing is diagnosed. Data is private by default: only what the astronaut confirms is packed as HL7 FHIR R4 and sent to a ground base, which shows it after a simulated communication delay. It runs locally, works without internet, and is open source (MIT license).
details:
What it does. PeWoNu (Peace, WOD, Nutrition) helps an astronaut understand their own wellbeing when the medical team is minutes away. It turns a few simple entries into a status for each indicator (green, amber, red or gray) and always says what that color was compared with. Each person is compared with their own baseline, kept separately for Earth, the spacecraft and a planet, and the system turns gray when it does not have enough data instead of guessing.

How it works. Peace: a five-face mood check; a guided "pulse mission" that teaches the wrist technique step by step and rewards good technique, never the value of the pulse; and an optional voice log that discards the audio and keeps only numeric measures, compared with the astronaut's own previous notes (no emotion is inferred). WOD: a workout of the day on the three machines of the International Space Station (T2 treadmill, CEVIS bike, ARED resistive device), built from age, weight and preflight bone density, with effort expressed as perceived exertion and no loads or doses. Nutrition: a daily energy estimate next to the 1,900 to 3,200 kcal range described by the Canadian Space Agency for station dietitians, and a meal log by ISS food type. The logic is deterministic: no AI model is in the alert path and nothing is diagnosed.

Privacy and the ground base. Data stays on the crew computer. Only what the astronaut chooses and confirms is packed as an HL7 FHIR R4 bundle (validated with the official HL7 validator, 0 errors) and sent to a ground base, which shows it after a configurable communication delay (default 12 minutes of simulated mission time; the real Earth-Mars one-way delay is about 3 to 22 minutes). The ground base never receives raw audio or conversations.

Benefits and impact. Fewer false alarms and less false reassurance, advice that fits each person and each environment, and a clear way to share only what the astronaut decides. It can also serve as a model for analog missions on Earth.

Tools. Python 3.12, Flet (interface, served locally and working offline), FastAPI and SQLite (ground base), sounddevice (microphone), a pure-Python core with a ports-and-adapters layout, pytest, ruff and mypy (strict), uv, the official HL7 FHIR validator, and Playwright for visual checks. Everything runs locally and installs with one command.

What is creative. The color is relative to the person, not to a population; gray is honest about missing data; the manual pulse becomes a guided game; the voice log keeps numbers instead of audio; and the workout and food pillars use the real ISS machines and food categories.

Factors we considered. Astronauts may fear that health reports affect mission selection, so reporting is private by default and escalation only suggests. The crew medical officer is not a physician, so we give sources and checklists, never diagnoses or doses. Communication with Earth is delayed, so the first decisions are made on board.

AI use: the code, tests and documentation were written with Claude Code; research notes were gathered with NotebookLM; the pulse-guide illustrations were generated with Gemini and edited with Meta AI; and the logo was generated with Gemini. AI-generated images carry a visible "AI-generated" mark.
